content: To prevent work-related mental health conditions, it is essential to implement psychosocial risk management strategies. These include organizational interventions aimed at improving working conditions, fostering a positive workplace culture, and enhancing interpersonal relationships among employees. Promoting and protecting mental health in the workplace can be achieved through targeted training programs. These programs should focus on improving mental health literacy, equipping workers with the skills to identify and address mental health issues, and empowering employees to seek support when needed. Supporting employees with mental health conditions is critical to ensuring their full and equitable participation in the workplace. This can be accomplished through reasonable accommodations, return-to-work programs, and supported employment initiatives. Creating an enabling environment for mental health at work requires cross-cutting actions. These include strong leadership, adequate investment, respect for workers' rights, integration of mental health into workplace policies, active participation of stakeholders, evidence-based practices, and compliance with regulations. As of 2022, nearly 60% of the global population is engaged in work. All workers have the right to a safe and healthy work environment. While work can positively influence mental health by providing structure, purpose, and social connections, it can also contribute to harm if the environment is unsafe or unhealthy. Mental health conditions affect not only workers but also their families, employers, and economies, regardless of whether these conditions are work-related. The relationship between mental health and work is deeply interconnected. A safe and healthy workplace supports mental well-being, while good mental health enables individuals to work productively. Conversely, an unsafe or unhealthy work environment can undermine mental health, and poor mental health can impair a person's ability to work effectively if left unsupported. Globally, 15% of working-age adults live with a mental health disorder, and without effective support systems, these conditions can lead to reduced self-confidence, job satisfaction, and productivity, as well as increased absenteeism and difficulty maintaining employment. Stigma and discrimination against individuals with mental health conditions remain widespread, creating barriers to employment and support. Many workers hesitate to disclose their mental health challenges or seek help due to fear of negative career consequences. Employers may also be reluctant to hire individuals with mental health conditions. This results in lost opportunities, reduced earnings, and broader societal costs, including increased unemployment, decreased productivity, and diminished tax revenue. Workplaces can either enhance or undermine mental health. Decent work provides income, structure, and a sense of purpose, which can positively impact mental health. For individuals with severe mental health conditions, employment can promote recovery, improve self-esteem, and enhance social functioning. However, unemployment, job insecurity, discrimination, and poor working conditions can be significant sources of stress and risk factors for mental health issues, including anxiety, depression, and even suicide. More than half of the global workforce operates in the informal economy, where there is often no regulatory protection for health and safety. These workers frequently endure unsafe working conditions, long hours, and limited access to social protections, all of which can undermine mental health and restrict access to care. Recent changes in the world of work, such as technological advancements, globalization, and the COVID-19 pandemic, have introduced new psychosocial risks or exacerbated existing ones. These changes have disrupted labor markets, increased financial instability, and led to widespread restructuring of businesses, further impacting workers' mental health. To address these challenges, effective policies and actions are needed to improve mental health at work. This includes preventing work-related mental health conditions, promoting mental well-being, and supporting all workers to participate fully and equitably in the workforce. Governments, employers, and other stakeholders must collaborate to create safe and healthy working environments, tackle stigma and discrimination, and implement evidence-based interventions. Governments play a crucial role in developing and enforcing laws and policies that protect mental health at work. This includes integrating mental health into occupational safety and health (OSH) frameworks, ensuring parity between mental and physical health, and providing guidance on managing psychosocial risks. Training programs for managers and workers are essential to building awareness and skills for recognizing and addressing mental health issues. Employers should also provide flexible working arrangements, modify workloads, and foster inclusive workplace cultures to support mental health. Organizational interventions, such as participatory approaches to job design and clear communication, can reduce emotional distress and improve job satisfaction, performance, and overall well-being. Ultimately, addressing mental health at work requires a comprehensive approach that combines prevention, protection, and support. By fostering a culture of inclusion, reducing stigma, and ensuring access to resources, workplaces can become environments that promote mental health and enable all workers to thrive.
